effect: New arms-industry capacity costs about a year of its output and takes years, not months. A new production line (ammunition, explosives, vehicles, aircraft, ships, missiles and the other military goods) cost 30% of one year's output at the added capacity and was ready in 6 months for ammunition and explosives, 18 for most goods and 36 for ships when the country already made the good; a first line, from no capacity at all, took 6 months whatever the good. Now a line costs one year's output, an expansion of an existing line takes 12 months for ammunition and explosives, 24 for most goods and 36 for ships, and a first line takes 24, 36 and 48 months. AI countries still start lines automatically on wartime demand and order backlogs, through the game's own gate: the firm pays what its cash allows and the state the rest, reserved in full at the start, and an AI starts a line only when the state's share is at most a quarter of its available military money (or within a public limit it has set). At the higher price fewer lines pass: in a 150-day comparison (seed 12345) AI countries started 68 lines instead of 97 (30% fewer, 38 countries instead of 45; those that started none at this price include Israel, North Korea and Pakistan, and Ukraine started 3 instead of 5). The procurement planner's wait for a producer without a line follows the new first-line months. Real-world basis: arms plants cost about one to two years of output and take two to five years (Western 155 mm shell capacity roughly doubled only two years after 2022; new shipyards and combat-aircraft lines take four years or more), and a first line in a country with no industry for the good is the slowest of all. Expected effect: running short of munitions and equipment in a war hurts for longer, and arms build-ups cost more. Day-0 effect: nothing changes at genesis; from the first month, countries that start lines (wars and order backlogs) pay more, wait longer, and some cannot afford a line they would have started. No new state.
